title: Interoperability vs. Security: Why not both?
body:
An open internet where people can freely build, share, and remix each other's work is a powerful engine of grassroots innovation we’ve all benefited from. In recent decades, however, corporations have taken control of an increasing share of this work, giving them a greater ability to stifle challengers and limit our choices. When regulators address this by mandating that  tech giants play fair by requiring interoperability, the gatekeepers respond with a tired refrain: Playing fair puts users’ security at risk.  
  Unfortunately for these trillion-dollar companies, this     gotcha     isn’t the end of the conversation. Regulators can ensure that meaningful choice    and    security thrive.  
  Lawmakers have been catching up, recognizing that the best way to rein in big tech is to require these    oligopolies    to open up their platforms to independent developers. As we    explained six years ago   , mandating interoperability helps prevent the misuse of people’s data and enables more privacy-respecting alternatives. Tech giants, in contrast, have been arguing that our data is safer when they have exclusive control.

title: EFF to Brazil’s ANPD: Data Privacy and Free Expression Must Underpin Platform Regulations
body:
The Brazilian National Data Protection Agency (ANPD) plays a pivotal role in the regulation of digital platforms according to new legislation approved in Brazil. Throughout this year, EFF has presented comments, filed submissions, and met with the agency to emphasize crucial guardrails that the enforcement of new regulations should ensure.     
  ANPD is responsible for detailing and applying obligations set in Law n. 15.211/2025, which established rules for the protection of children and adolescents in the digital space. While some provisions establish important privacy safeguards, like prohibiting advertising based on profiling of underage users, the law created mandatory age assurance mechanisms for accessing digital products and services.     
  We have   raised alarms   on the privacy and free expression issues around age-gating the internet.   Age verification technology is often    inaccurate    and    privacy-invasive   .    Examples also show    how it’s prone to enforcement overreach, resulting in sites blocked beyond legal requirements. title: EFF’s State Legislative Agenda to End ALPR Mass Surveillance
body: Police agencies across the U.S. have deployed Automated License Plate Readers (ALPRs) to capture images of passing vehicles along with time, date, and GPS coordinates. While the technology itself isn’t new (ALPRs have existed in various forms for  more than 50 years , and in  the U.S. since 1998 ), the surveillance landscape has shifted dramatically. Rapid advances in artificial intelligence and national data sharing have transformed police ALPRs into an interconnected, nationwide tracking network. It is pitched to city councils by law enforcement and private vendors like Flock Safety, Motorola Solutions (Vigilant), and Axon as an essential tool for solving violent crime.  In reality, it is an inherently dangerous infrastructure of mass surveillance.  Since  2012 , EFF has worked with others to expose the severe digital rights harms of ALPR systems. For example, we’ve recently documented how these camera networks allow law enforcement to  search for immigrants ,  track peaceful protesters , target  Romani communities , and  track women seeking reproductive healthcare . title: Victory! Court Rules OPM Data Disclosure to DOGE Is Unlawful
body:
In a victory for data privacy,  a federal court in New York definitively ruled  that the Office of Personnel Management (OPM) violated the law when it disclosed millions of federal employee records to DOGE agents. In a summary judgment ruling issued on October 20, 2026, the court found that OPM violated two provisions of the Privacy Act—one restricting disclosure of personal records between agencies and another requiring agencies to protect the security and confidentiality of records. 
 Since the case was filed, many DOGE agents have left the government and OPM has rescinded their database access. However, OPM should still clean up the cybersecurity mess it created. The court will decide the remedy at a later date. 
 "By virtue of the Court’s summary judgment ruling, OPM’s decision to grant DOGE Agents broad access to its systems of recordings containing [personally identifiable information (PII)] has been held unlawful," Judge Denise Cote wrote. 
 "The record also provides no support for a finding that it was the pursuit of a modernization agenda that prompted OPM to grant sweeping and expedited access to a score of DOGE Agents to its systems of records containing PII," she added.

title: Require Police to Get a Warrant to Search ALPR Data
body:
This post was co-written by     Andi Cao    , an EFF legal intern.  
 Automated license plate readers (ALPRs) are mass surveillance. They photograph every passing car and log where and when it was captured, building a searchable record of where nearly everyone drives.   Cities should not buy them  , and cities that already have them should shut them down. 
 Where these systems still operate, courts and state legislatures must reduce their harms by (among other things) requiring police to get a warrant before searching stored ALPR data. A warrant requirement would not make mass surveillance acceptable, but it would require police to justify a search to a judge before accessing records of people’s movements. Without this independent judicial check on police power, officers have been searching this data for improper reasons (many exposed by EFF) that violate our fundamental rights. 
 A warrant requires a judge to find probable cause and specificity—many warrantless police searches of ALPR data lack both. title: In Memoriam: Barry Steinhardt
body:
Barry Steinhardt, a lifelong privacy champion and an early leader in the battle for digital civil liberties who served as EFF’s president in 1998-99, died last week at age 73.     
  A Connecticut native, Steinhardt led the Vermont and Pennsylvania affiliates of the American Civil Liberties Union before becoming associate director of the national ACLU. There, he helped spearhead the fight to overturn much of the Communications Decency Act, resulting in the U.S. Supreme Court’s landmark     Reno v. ACLU     ruling in 1997.     
  When the internet was still young,   Steinhardt   became one of   the first   attorneys to   specialize in the intersection of technology and privacy  .   In early 1998 he took a leave of absence from the ACLU to become EFF’s president, and then returned to the ACLU in 1999.     
  In 2002 he founded the ACLU’s Program on Technology and Liberty. After retiring from the ACLU, he continued on as a senior advisor to London-based  Privacy International .

Law enforcement entities throughout Wisconsin collect, store, share, and aggregate this ALPR data. Then they search it, retrospectively tracking the movements of individuals and entire communities in ways that would have been prohibitively costly, if not outright impossible, before the advent of ALPR technology.

title: DHS Inspector General Finds That TSA is Not Properly Safeguarding Passenger Facial Recognition Data
body:

  The Department of Homeland Security Office of Inspector General (DHS OIG) has    published a summary of findings    from its audit of the Transportation Security Administration’s (TSA) facial recognition technology. While the detailed findings are classified, the summary states that the OIG’s audit uncovered a “significant weakness” in the technology’s ability to protect the privacy of passenger data. title: As Federal Court Rules ALPRs are Mass Surveillance, EFF Gets Disappointing Ruling
body:
In an extremely disappointing  ruling , a California trial court dismissed   SIREN v. San Jose  , our case challenging the city of San Jose’s warrantless searches of its vast stores of automated license plate reader (ALPR) data. EFF and the ACLU of Northern California represent SIREN and CAIR California, two non-profits that serve San Jose residents, in this case. 
 Make no mistake: We believe this ruling is wrong on the law, and we will appeal. The ruling ignores the importance of landmark rulings from the U.S. Supreme Court regarding the invasiveness of aggregating collected data on an individual over time, including  one issued just months ago . It also severely underestimates the harm that ALPRs cause, in San Jose and around the country.  
 San Jose’s ALPR surveillance system is inescapable. It blankets the city’s streets in nearly five hundred cameras that continuously photograph every car that passes by and retains the collected data for a month or longer. In our briefs, we argued that law enforcement officers who warrantlessly search the resulting ALPR database are violating the California Constitution’s ban on unreasonable searches and its guarantee of privacy. title: Privacy's Defenders Podcast: No Privacy Without Encryption
body:
When we communicate online today – from your personal emails and DMs to secure international commerce – we usually do so with encryption. Encryption converts readable data into unreadable gibberish to protect our privacy and security. This didn’t just happen organically. Three decades ago, the U.S government treated encryption like a weapon, and it took some unlikely heroes to set it free: a grad student, a junior lawyer, and a fledgling digital rights group who sued the federal government.     
  The ruling in     Bernstein v. Department of Justice     held that code is speech and so is protected by the First Amendment – a precedent that underpins the internet as we know it today. This landmark case was led by Cindy Cohn, then a young pro bono lawyer working on behalf of EFF, who went on to become EFF’s legal director and then executive director.     
  Welcome to the second episode of “Privacy’s Defenders,” a podcast about the people – lawyers, journalists, hackers, and others – who’ve fought to secure your digital liberties since before most people even knew what the internet was.

title: Resisting the Menace of Federal Data Consolidation
body:
In the past two years, the federal government has unlawfully  consolidated data  exposing our private information.  
 This consolidation has been chaotic but generally came in three rolling waves: It started with DOGE, moved to agency-to-agency data sharing with ICE, and then attempted data-driven purges of state voter rolls. 
 We all deserve to live in a world where the data we use to pay our taxes, receive benefits, and vote is not combined and weaponized against us. The amalgamation of data leads to mistakes, abuses, and a lack of trust in institutions meant to protect us. Overall, it can chill our participation in society. This is particularly true for groups disfavored by this administration—especially immigrants and protesters. 
 Congress highlighted similar abuses—including the creation of enemies lists and snooping on activists and federal employees—following the McCarthy and Watergate eras. And the increasing use of computers to magnify those harms led Congress to pass a slate of protections like the federal  Privacy Act  of 1974.

title: The Cloud and AI Development Act (CADA) represents everything that’s wrong with Europe’s approach to digital sovereignty
body:
The EU’s Tech Sovereignty Package is supposed to jump-start Europe’s “sovereign AI” ambitions.  But due to fundamental misunderstandings about the technology behind ‘AI’ and the blind trust in Big Tech’s AI doomer and boomer narratives, it is more likely to instead hurt digital rights and the environment instead, and waste valuable public resources that should have been invested in actually increasing Europe’s digital resilience. The Cloud and AI Development (CADA) Act, a part of the Tech Sovereignty Package, adds up to an aggressive policy push to impose “European AI”.

title: Greece Enacts Social Media Ban For Kids Under 15
body:
Greece has passed a law banning children under 15 from social media platforms beginning January 1, 2027. The legislation requires platforms to implement reliable age verification and parents to use government-backed apps to restrict access, with penalties for noncompliance under the EU's Digital Services Act. Engadget reports: "It would have been very easy to do absolutely nothing today and wait for the perfect European law. But the challenge is here. Children are sinking into the internet every day, and I believe a responsible government must do what it is obliged to do," said Greece's digital governance and AI minister, Dimitris Papastergiou.
 
The legislation was opposed by Greece's minority parties, so Mitsotakis used his majority government to pass the bill. The nation previously barred mobile phones in schools in 2024, and opinion polls show that the new social media ban for children is widely supported by Greece's adult population. Mitsotakis previously said that his government's "goal is to push the European Union in this direction as well."

title: Left Alone With Nothing To Do, AI Agents Started Playing
body:
An anonymous reader quotes a report from TechCrunch: AI agents left to explore a virtual island without a specific task began inventing challenges of their own. MIT researchers say the behavior bears the hallmarks of play. The researchers put 13 AI agents called Eko, each running on Claude Opus 4.7, alone on a simulated desert island for 30 hours. They describe the experiment in a paper posted on arXiv, a site where researchers share studies before peer review. Afterward, they gave the agents specific challenges, like getting as many objects as possible onto the island's tallest rock spire. The Eko agents that had spent those 30 hours playing generally beat identical agents that had never set foot on the island.
 
Today, developers decide in advance what AI should practice and what counts as success. The researchers see this technique -- exploring without a goal -- as a different way for AI agents to learn skills, especially skills that could one day be used to control robots. "We normally develop artificial agents by deciding in advance what they should practice, what they should optimize, and what counts as progress," the researchers write in their report. title: Physicists Trap a Single Antimatter Particle For a Month
body:
Physicists at Northwestern University have successfully trapped a single positron for an entire month, allowing researchers to study its quantum properties with unprecedented precision. "Further investigations using the trap might reveal the secret of why the world around us is made of matter and not antimatter, when things could have presumably gone either way," reports Scientific American. From the report: Every normal particle of matter has an antimatter counterpart with equal mass but opposite charge. To build their trap, physicists started with atoms of sodium 22, a radioactive isotope with a half-life of about two and a half years. When one of these atoms decays, it emits a positron -- the antimatter counterpart of the electron. title: UN Says Breaching 1.5C Warming Limit Is 'Imminent and Unavoidable'
body:
For the first time, the UN has declared that exceeding the Paris Agreement's 1.5C warming limit is "imminent and unavoidable." "We are now saying this window has closed, but we can open it again by making the overshoot as brief as possible," UN Environment Program Executive Director Inger Andersen said on a call with reporters. "This is about how to find a way back as shortly and as quickly as possible with as limited an overshoot as possible." CNN reports: Past reports have examined the distance between countries' emissions reduction commitments and what it would take to limit global warming to 1.5 C above preindustrial levels. However, this year's report redefines the gap. Instead, it examines new emissions overshoot scenarios, and what it would take to limit peak warming to just 1.7 to 1.8 degrees C before bringing temperatures back down to 1.5 C through emissions cuts and the use of carbon removal technologies.

title: To Make Way For Data Centers, Google Will Pay Others to Use Less Power
body:
Google is funding one of the nation's largest "virtual power plants," paying homes and businesses indirectly to reduce electricity consumption during periods of peak demand so more grid capacity can be available for data centers. Under its expanded deal with Voltus, the program could provide up to 1,070 megawatts in the Mid-Atlantic PJM grid -- roughly the output of a large nuclear reactor. The New York Times reports: That electricity won't come from new power plants. Instead, Voltus will sign up homes and businesses and give them financial incentives to curb their usage when local power demand is high or the grid is strained. Many of these reductions could occur automatically, such as through smart thermostats that dial back air-conditioning during peak summer hours or batteries that can provide temporary on-site power.
 
Each of these tweaks frees up only a small amount of power on its own. But by aggregating them across thousands of businesses and homes, Voltus says it can reliably provide lots of extra capacity when it's most needed, and do so within a few years. title: Microsoft Says October Updates Didn't Actually Fix VPN Issues
body:
joshuark shares a report from BleepingComputer: Microsoft says it mistakenly flagged a bug causing Always On VPN connection issues as fixed in the October 2026 Windows 11 cumulative updates. Always On VPN replaced the legacy DirectAccess technology and supports domain-joined, non-domain-joined, and Microsoft Entra ID-joined devices running Windows 10, Windows 11, and Windows Server. It runs in the background and establishes secure tunnels back to the user's corporate network whenever their device connects to the internet.
 
Microsoft first acknowledged the issue in a service alert sent to IT administrators in late September, saying it was triggered on systems running Windows 11 24H2 and later after installing the September 2026 security updates when the initial Always On VPN connection failed (e.g., when using automatic protocol selection with IKEv2 and SSTP). "When automatic protocol selection or protocol fallback was configured, affected VPN connections could remain stuck in a Connecting state or fail to connect after an initial connection attempt failed," it said. "In some cases, subsequent connection attempts could display the error, 'The specified port is already in use.'"

title: Today's PHP Security Release, and How We're Strengthening PHP Security (PHP Foundation)
body:
The PHP Foundation has put out  a
blog entry  explaining how the vulnerabilities disclosed today came
about and why they took so long to fix.
 
 
	To fix the OOM problem, the PHP security team developed several
	competing approaches, but each came with its own trade-offs:
	backward compatibility breaks, new denial-of-service potential, or
	requiring changes to many third-party extensions which seemed
	impossible to coordinate. The PHP security team, operating on
	consensus, struggled to choose between these and feared the
	repercussions of shipping the wrong choice. Combined with the lack
	of a known path to remote code execution and the small team of core
	developers with the necessary deep knowledge of the engine occupied
	with many responsibilities, this decision process caused work on a
	fix to stall and restart repeatedly over months. We won't pretend
	otherwise: the delay was a structural failure, caused by both the
	security team's decision process and its lack of resources.

The Node.js project has

 musl libc project  has also announced a

 out-of-bounds

title: [$] Hash-based module integrity for reproducible distributions
body:
We last looked in on  hash-based integrity
checking for kernel modules  just over a year and half ago.  Since that time,
the  patch
set  has undergone multiple revisions.  At the 2026  Linux Plumbers Conference 
(LPC),  Thomas Weißschuh described the need for kernel-module integrity
guarantees while still providing reproducible builds, how his patches implement that, and some ideas for possible
further work.

title: Upstreaming Tyr: Rust, DRM, and the Linux Kernel (Collabora)
body:
The Collabora blog  provides
an update on Tyr , a driver for Arm Mali GPUs.
 
 
	One of our biggest challenges has been developing Tyr while the
	Rust kernel abstractions and driver interfaces are also being
	developed. As the driver interfaces are naturally revised and
	improved, we have rewritten Tyr several times to adapt to the
	larger Rust ecosystem. This not only makes progress much slower
	than it would be with a mature API, but also stalls progress for
	capabilities, such as job scheduling, while the abstraction is
	properly designed, reviewed, tested, and merged upstream.
 
	But working in this evolving environment is also precisely where
	Tyr is able to provide the most value. As a user of these new Rust
	abstractions, Tyr helps to expose their requirements and
	limitations.

title: [$] Understanding Nix flakes
body:
Nix flakes  are an
experimental feature of the  Nix package-management
tool  designed to build projects in a more self-contained and reproducible
way. Despite the feature's experimental status, it has become increasingly
popular for open-source projects to publish  flake.nix  files that offer
predefined development environments and build automation even when those
repositories may not offer an upstream package or module for the  NixOS Linux distribution . Although
Nix flakes have a complicated history, and the path for stabilization is
uncertain, flakes can provide useful capabilities for projects that choose to
include them.

title: PHP patches released for two critical RCEs
body:
The PHP project has  published  PHP
versions  8.5.12 ,
 8.4.27 ,  8.3.36  and  8.2.35  to address
two critical vulnerabilities that could allow unauthenticated remote code
execution. 

 
 Who is at risk:  all PHP installations serving web requests,
including PHP-FPM, Apache with mod_php, php-cgi, FrankenPHP and LiteSpeed. We
consider the risk highest for mod_php, with a demonstrated exploit where an
unauthenticated request can trigger the attack before any application code
runs. 

  The vulnerabilities:  

 
  RCE via OOM corruption , CVE-2026-109618 ( GHSA-w8hw-w9fx-j79w ): out-of-memory
handling can interrupt PHP while internal request data is only partially initialized. Request cleanup may then treat the invalid data as valid. 
  RCE via stale global state , CVE-2026-109619 ( GHSA-6wmf-4rv5-p3rp ): request-owned
internal state can survive after its backing memory has been freed. A later
request handled by the same worker may use that stale state before normal
initialization resets it. 
 
 

 PHP versions older than 8.1 will not receive updates from the project, though
the project has provided some patches for  PHP
7.4 ,  PHP
8.0 , and  PHP
8.1  to assist in creating backports. A

title: Google ML Kit's barcode scanner adds the INTERNET permission and sends diagnostics, even in apps with no network code
body:
While checking one of my own apps with Exodus Privacy, I noticed it had the INTERNET permission even though the code never touches the network. The culprit turned out to be Google ML Kit's barcode scanning library, which a very popular Flutter QR scanner uses under the hood. It adds INTERNET and ACCESS_NETWORK_STATE through a Google transport library, and sends diagnostic data to Google when the scanner is opened (device model, app version, an install-scoped ID, latencies, error codes). Google documents this, but you'd never guess it from an app that just reads a QR code.

A few things I took away from it:
- A "0 trackers" result on Exodus doesn't mean "no network". Check the permission list too.
- If an app that should be offline asks for INTERNET, a QR/barcode feature is worth suspecting.
- For developers: ZXing-based scanners decode entirely on-device and don't pull any of this in. You can confirm with the merged manifest or the manifest-merger report in your build folder.

Has anyone else run into libraries quietly adding network access like this? Curious which others are common offenders.

title: Let's Encrypt to Cut SSL Certificate Lifetimes to 64 Days in February 2027
body:

>
>All certificates issued or renewed from that date will have a 64-day lifespan unless users explicitly select one of the shorter options already available: 45 or six days.
>
>Existing certificates will remain valid until their expiration dates. Let’s Encrypt expects the final 90-day certificate to expire on May 11, 2027. The organization also confirmed no valid certificates will be revoked during the transition.
>
>To help administrators prepare, Let’s Encrypt will introduce 64-day certificates in its staging environment on October 14, 2026, allowing users to test their renewal setups before the change reaches production.
>
>The move is part of a broader effort to improve web security by reducing how long compromised or incorrectly issued certificates remain usable. Simply put, shorter certificate lifetimes mean attackers have less time to exploit a stolen private key.

title: Show HN: ADRs for AI – Deliberation records for human–AI work, versioned in Git
body:
Why is this worth your time? Essentially, this solves two problems of AI-assisted programming:

(a) the first problem is how to do oversight and what do oversight of and this is solved through the ORRCF (for Options, Recommendation, Rationale, Confidence, Falsifier) question format (in which models are supposed to surface all their doubts with fully fleshed out recommendations, with falsifier, to be approved or overridden)

(b) the second problem is how to scaffold sustainable AI-written code; the ADRs (Architectural Deliberation Records, after Nygard's decision records) written by the models, summarize all the thought process involved in any design decision and provides the blueprint for the code.

In tandem, the records provide both the reason why certain non-obvious design choices were made, from a constant, to a library choice, to an ordering in an operation; and also under what conditions different decisions would be made, for instance, in a different platform, or under different latency requirements, or for a different audience, and so on.

This is a framework I've been working for over a year, that is the starting point of all my projects.

title: Show HN: Check if any of the $656M in unclaimed royalties at The MLC is yours
body:
Hi HN, I built this. Quick background on why it exists:

When music is streamed on digital streaming platforms (think Spotify, Apple Music, Pandora), there are two separate royalty streams: one for the recording, paid through your distributor (DistroKid, TuneCore, CDBaby), and one for the underlying work (generally known as publishing). The work side's mechanical royalties are collected by The MLC, a nonprofit that was created by the 2018 Music Modernization Act (MMA). If you haven't registered your songs with The MLC, there are issues with your metadata, or about half a dozen other reasons, that money will never reach you, it just collects in a big pile we call the "black box".

That pile is big. The MLC's own dashboard currently shows over $656M is held (themlc.com/blanket-royalties), and the biggest problem is the MMA dictates that The MLC cannot hold that money indefinitely. At some point, by law, The MLC must distribute this big pile of cash, and since they don't know who it's supposed to go to, they pay it out through a process called "market share" (themlc.com/marketshare). title: How to reliably retrieve all posts from a Facebook group going back to 2015 (search misses results, scrolling crashes around 2022)
body:
I'm a member of a Facebook group that has been posting content (trivia questions) since 2015, and I want to catalogue every post starting from the earliest one. 
 Problem 1 : Search is unreliable: Using Facebook's built-in search within the group doesn't return all posts from a given year. Some posts are omitted for no apparent reason, even when filtering by date. 
 Problem 2 : Scrolling crashes: Manually scrolling back through the group's history works up to a point, but once I reach posts from around 2022, the browser tab/app consistently crashes before I can get further back. 
 Constraint: The posts don't share consistent keywords or phrasing, so text-based search isn't a reliable filter. Filtering by month/year seems like the only practical approach, but I can't get it to work reliably.
What I'm looking for: 
 A reliable method or tool to filter/export Facebook group posts by date range
Any way to export or archive a group's full post history (browser extension, API, third-party tool, etc.) 
 A workaround for the crashing when scrolling through several years of content 
 Has anyone dealt with this before, and what worked for you?

title: 'Action Required' Sign in to Google Photos with your Google Account to keep your photos & videos
body:
I get these emails frequently with subject line "[Action Required] Sign in to Google Photos with your Google Account to keep your photos & videos". Every time it's from a different email. It seems to  be click bait and a security issue but there is no CVE related to it. 
 The email message contains 
 
 This is a copy of a security alert sent to <some_username@gmail.com>.
<myactualemail@gmail.com> is the recovery email for this account. If
you don't recognize this account, remove it. 
 
 But my email shouldn't be the recovery email of any of these accounts. 
 If anyone thinks all of a sudden, 50 different people are sharing photos with me, that's not normal. Does someone understand what this is? And why is Google not doing anything about this when their platform is being abused?
